summary: EPP predates internationalized email addresses and does not support them directly. This document defines a command-response extension that lets a contact object carry an additional email address, so such addresses can be stored and used.

plainLanguage.summary: Some people have a second mailbox, and some names use letters from other alphabets. This lets domain systems store an extra email address for a contact.

questions: what is the epp additional email extension
how does epp support internationalized email
what does the primary attribute do in epp
subtitle: An EPP extension that lets a contact object carry a second email address, ASCII or internationalized.

tldr.problem: EPP was designed before internationalized email addresses existed, so its contact object cannot hold an SMTPUTF8 address.
tldr.mechanism: A command-response extension adds an addlEmail element to the contact create, update and info operations, holding one additional email address that can be ASCII-only or SMTPUTF8 and can be marked as primary.
tldr.outcome: Clients and servers signal support in login and greeting using a namespace URI. Without that negotiation, extended contact objects must not be sent or returned.

today: RFC 9873 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the EPP contact mapping of RFC 5733 and is registered as an Active EPP extension.

sections.title: Why EPP Needs an Additional Email
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730) is used to manage objects such as contacts. Its contact mapping (RFC 5733) holds a single email address. This document defines a command-response extension that adds a second one, which can be an ASCII-only address or an internationalized SMTPUTF8 address (RFC 6530).

The second address can serve as an ASCII fallback if delivery to the primary address fails, or as an SMTPUTF8 address for contact purposes with the ASCII address as the fallback. The extension does not change any other EPP extension that includes an email address. Adding SMTPUTF8 support there would need updates to those specifications.

When a contact has two addresses, users should be aware that either address may be forwarded to the other, so a message sent to one may get a reply from the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Your school card has room for one phone number. This adds a second one, and the second one is allowed to be written in any alphabet.

sections.title: Email Address Syntax
sections.content:
The base contact mapping points to RFC 5322 for email syntax, which does not cover internationalized addresses. SMTPUTF8 address syntax comes from Section 3.3 of RFC 6531. It extends the SMTP Mailbox, Local-part and Domain rules to allow UTF8-non-ascii characters in the local part and U-labels in the domain.

The validation rules in RFC 6531 MUST be followed when processing internationalized email addresses in this extension.
sections.plainLanguage: An address in another alphabet still has to follow spelling rules. This says which rulebook to check it against.

sections.title: The Additional Email Element
sections.content:
The extension adds one element, <addlEmail:addlEmail>, with a single child, <addlEmail:email>. It holds the second address. An empty <addlEmail:email/> unsets the address in an update and means "not set" in an info response.

The element has an optional primary attribute. It marks the extension address as the primary one for the contact. It MUST NOT be present when the element is empty. In the schema it is a boolean with a default of false.

Two further rules apply. The flag attribute of <contact:disclose><contact:email/> MUST also be applied to all additional addresses. And the extension address is associated only with the primary <contact:email>; support for any further addresses MUST explicitly describe how they are associated.
sections.plainLanguage: The second slot can be left empty, and a small sticker can say that this one is now the main address.

sections.title: Signaling and Negotiation
sections.content:
Support is signaled with the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:addlEmail-1.0. The client lists it in an <svcExtension><extURI> element of the <login> command, and the server lists it in the same element of the greeting.

When the extension is negotiated, the server MUST accept SMTPUTF8 addresses, validate them with the rules above, store internationalized characters, return them in responses, and support the SMTP extension of RFC 6531 when sending or receiving email. The client MUST provide and accept SMTPUTF8 addresses and support the same SMTP extension.

When the extension is not negotiated, an extended contact object MUST NOT be provided or returned by either side.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides first say whether they understand the new slot. If they do not both say yes, nobody uses it.

sections.title: How the Commands Change
sections.content:
The extension touches only three operations. In an info response the server adds the <addlEmail:addlEmail> element next to the normal result data. In a create command the extension element MUST be present to set the alternate address. In an update command it MUST be present to set or unset it, and if the address cannot be applied the server MUST return EPP error result code 2201.

The check, delete, renew and transfer commands and responses, and the create and update responses, get no new elements. The RFC's examples show an ASCII alternate address, an SMTPUTF8 address marked primary="true", and an update that unsets the address.
sections.plainLanguage: You can read the second slot, fill it in when making a card, or change or clear it later. Nothing else about the card's handling changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unconstrained Unicode in email addresses can create threats that ASCII-only addresses do not, as RFC 6530 notes. Because addresses passed in EPP are displayed in the Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) and other services, and are often copied and pasted when businesses transfer domains, SMTPUTF8 addresses SHOULD be used with policies that disallow unconstrained Unicode. The domain part SHOULD conform to IDNA2008, and the local part SHOULD be restricted to Unicode that avoids those threats, for example by disallowing characters outside Unicode Annex 31.

A malicious actor could register a valid domain with a similar U-label (a homograph attack) and take control of the domain through social engineering. So registries SHOULD validate the domain syntax in addresses and check that it uses the code points listed in the IANA "IDNA Rules and Derived Property Values" registry. The RFC also warns that local parts are very liberal, and that implementers may wish to test that their database can store difficult ones.
sections.plainLanguage: Lookalike letters from other alphabets can trick people. Registries should check addresses carefully so a copycat cannot grab someone's mail.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content: The content of <addlEmail:email> elements can be processed and published, for example through RDAP, in the same way as <contact:email>. Many data protection regulations treat email addresses as personal data, so policies for collecting, transmitting and processing contact information should apply equally to the additional address.
sections.plainLanguage: An email address is personal information, so the second one deserves the same care as the first.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:addlEmail-1.0 and the XML schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:epp:addlEmail-1.0, both with the IESG as registrant contact. The extension is also registered in the EPP extension registry (RFC 7451) with the status Active and TLDs set to Any.
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists now include this extension, so everyone uses the same names for it.
